t: Check if an Array Is Consecutive — Sorting vs Hash Set
o: An array is consecutive when its distinct values form the exact integer range [min, min + n - 1] with no gaps or duplicates. [1,3,4,2] qualifies because sorted it is 1,2,3,4; [1,3] fails since 2 is missing; [3,5,4] qualifies as 3,4,5. With $n$ up to $10^5$, either sorting and verifying adjacent differences, or checking uniqueness plus the span condition, both fit easily in limits. The two checks in the hash approach are jointly sufficient: n distinct values spanning exactly n-1 must be precisely the integers in between.
k: Sorted consecutive means every adjacent difference equals exactly 1.
Equivalently: all elements are distinct AND max - min == n - 1 — together these force the set to be {min, ..., min+n-1}.
The hash-set test avoids the O(n log n) sort and runs in linear time.

a.n: Approach 1: Sort and Verify Adjacent Steps
a.i: After sorting ascending, a consecutive array satisfies nums[i+1] - nums[i] == 1 everywhere; any duplicate yields a 0 gap and any hole yields a gap > 1. This is the simplest correct strategy and matches the natural mental model of laying values in order.
s: Scan adjacent pairs; if any difference is not 1, return false.
Return true if the whole scan passes.
a.t: O(n log n) — dominated by the sort; the verification scan is linear.
a.sp: O(1) extra — in-place sort (ignoring sort's internal stack).

a.n: Approach 2: Hash Set with Span Check
a.i: Skip sorting entirely: insert everything into a set to detect duplicates, and track min and max. If the set size equals n and max - min equals n - 1, the n distinct integers occupy exactly the n slots of the range, so every value in it appears. This achieves linear time at the cost of hash-set memory.
s: Insert all elements into a hash set while tracking mn and mx.
If set size != n, there is a duplicate — return false.
a.t: O(n) — one pass to build the set and find extremes (expected, hashing).
a.sp: O(n) — the hash set stores all elements.

w: Use Approach 1 as the quick default; mention Approach 2 when asked to beat O(n log n), noting the memory trade-off. Pitfalls: in JavaScript use a comparator (nums.sort() alone sorts lexicographically); duplicates break the naive 'max - min == n - 1' check unless distinctness is verified too; a single-element array is trivially consecutive (both approaches return true). Follow-ups: handle near-sorted input with an O(n) counting/bitmap method when the value range is bounded, or check consecutiveness without modifying the input.
